def: A systematic error that does not shrink with more data. The opposite of noise.
Resample your data with replacement many times to see how much an estimate would wobble.
You know a value exceeded some cap but not by how much. Timeouts and token limits create this.
Averages tend toward a bell shape regardless of the raw data's shape, with variance shrinking as one over n.
A range produced by a procedure that captures the truth a stated share of the time.
A task where two models disagreed. The only tasks that carry information in a paired test.
How big the difference is, as opposed to how confident you are that it exists.
Spread that changes with the value. Common in latency: slow things vary more.
Intraclass correlation: the share of variance that lives between clusters rather than within them.
Interquartile range: the middle 50% of the data, p75 minus p25. Outliers cannot move it.
How heavy the tails are. High kurtosis means extremes are more common than a bell predicts.
How long you have already waited tells you nothing about the remaining wait. True of the exponential and geometric.
Count data with variance well above its mean. Poisson does not apply; use negative binomial or bootstrap.
The same tasks were given to both models, so comparisons can use within-task differences.
The value below which a given share of the data falls. p95 is the 0.95 quantile.
The chance of detecting a real effect of a given size, if it exists.
How often you would see a result this extreme if there were genuinely no effect. Not the probability the null is true.
What you believed before seeing this data. With small samples it does real work in a Bayesian estimate.
A score minimised by reporting your true belief. Brier score is one; ECE is not.
Resistant to outliers. The median is robust, the mean is not.
The spread of results you would get from repeating the whole experiment on fresh samples.
Asymmetry, named for the side the tail is on. Mean divided by median above 1.2 signals right skew.
Typical distance of a single measurement from the mean. Does not shrink with more data.
Typical distance of your estimate from the truth. Shrinks as one over the square root of n.
Standard deviation squared. Adds cleanly across independent sources.
Cap extreme values at a percentile rather than removing them. Justified only for confirmed measurement errors.
The arithmetic average: add everything, divide by n. Right for totals, misleading on skewed data.
The middle value when sorted. The robust centre for skewed data like latency.
The most common value. Useful for categories and for spotting two humps.
Median absolute deviation: the median distance from the median. Multiply by 1.4826 to compare with the sd.
Probability density function: how common values are around each point. The familiar humped curve.
Cumulative distribution function: the share of values at or below each point. Rises from 0 to 1.
A plot of your data's quantiles against a reference distribution's. A straight line means a good match.
Two or more populations sharing an axis, often visible as two humps. Split them before summarising.
The distribution of a quantity whose log is normal. Arises from multiplicative effects; the shape of latency and token counts.
A count distribution with variance above the mean, arising when the event rate varies across units. Fits tool calls per session.
A distribution with no typical size, straight on log-log axes. Its mean may not exist; report percentiles only.
A confidence interval for a proportion that stays inside 0 to 1 and behaves well at small n and extreme rates.
The exponential of the average log. On lognormal data it equals the median.
The mean after dropping a fixed share from each end. Rarely right for a one-sided tail.
Methods such as Kaplan-Meier that handle censored data correctly, for example requests cut off by a timeout.
